entries.title: With an ad aimed at Trump, this Republican exposed GOP angst about Latino voters
entries.summary: Rep. María Elvira Salazar filmed an ad warning the president that he's "gone too far" on immigration. It reflected concern among some Republicans that their gains with Latino voters could be at risk.
entries.content:
With an ad aimed at Trump, this Republican exposed GOP angst about Latino voters

MIAMI – At the heart of Little Havana neighborhood here, is Máximo Gómez Park, also known as Domino Park. Cuban Americans play games of dominos here to escape the pressures of daily life.

But what started as a typical day at the park last week took a turn: Miami police arrested a player in the middle of a game after a dispute with a city worker. It spurred other players to worry about deportations, setting off a broader political debate over whether President Trump or former President Biden was responsible for a higher cost of living.

"It's Biden," said Alejandro Torres, a Republican voter.

"It's Trump," responded Ricardo Carracedo, who plans to vote for Democrats in the midterm elections.

This same divide is playing out across Florida's 27th Congressional District, a Miami-Dade County seat that is more than 70% Latino. It is a warning for Republicans, whose 2024 wins relied heavily on this crucial electorate.

That year, Trump cut Democrats' margin with Latino voters nationally to just three points – down from 25 points four years earlier, according to Pew Research Center. Cuban Americans, the district's largest Latino group, have been reliable Trump supporters. But many of their friends and relatives have been swept up by the administration's deportation agenda. A crack among them could signal broader trouble for Latino support for Republican candidates.

Rep. María Elvira Salazar, a Cuban-American Republican in her third term, has been sounding the alarm. Last month, Salazar filmed a television ad in front of the White House warning President Trump that he's "gone too far" on immigration.

"The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today," she said.

Trump hit back at Salazar after the ad. On his TruthSocial account, he shared a post in which another user called her a "back stabber."

Salazar told NPR she didn't see the comments as attacks, saying she later spoke to the president.

"I told him, 'You know, what I'm telling you is what my people are feeling,'" she said. "This is Democracy where we tell the boss, 'hey, this is what's happening in my neck of the woods.' And that's exactly what I did."

Salazar's read of the effect of Trump's policies may be right. Polling firm Equis Research found in a recent survey of registered voters who identify as Hispanic or Latino that if the election for Congress were held today, voters would pick the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a margin of 57 to 31.

At a Salazar campaign event this past Thursday, friends Mirla Loredo and Ramona Tunon were divided on whether they sided with her take or Trump's.

"Him, I tell you," Loredo said in Spanish.

"I like her position," Tunon said.

Salazar has pushed against aggressive immigration policies in the past. For several years, she has proposed legislation she called the Dignity Act to block deportations of immigrants considered pillars of their community – such as hospitality, construction and farm workers.

Still, Carracedo, the Democratic voter from Domino Park, said he'll vote a straight blue ticket. He said Salazar's recent push against Trump's aggressive deportations is too little, too late.

"I'm not going to vote for her, because at the last hour she's defending Hispanics. But the entire time she supported Trump and the money Trump wanted for ICE," or Immigration and Customs Enforcement, he said in his native Spanish.

Trump, he said, reminds him of the communist leaders he left behind in Cuba.

In the past, Republicans' messaging on socialism had a powerful impact on this district. But now that message has lost some of its potency, eclipsed by worries about a higher cost of living and deportations.

Eduardo Gamarra, a politics professor at Florida International University, says the local economy's malaise has eclipsed all other issues.

"It's probably the number one thing. And that cuts across all of the electorate," he said.

He said the second top issue is deportations, which have devastated some Miami businesses that have lost workers and customers.

An opening for Democrats

Salazar's Democratic challenger, Eliott Rodriguez, is a former broadcast journalist with Cuban roots like Salazar. He says he wants to revamp the immigration judge system, and restore federal food assistance after cuts that have hurt constituents.

Still, he concedes his party has a lot of ground to make up after largely walking away from Florida.

"One of the biggest mistakes that Democrats have made in Florida is to think that Florida is unwinnable. But I beg to differ."

Polls in the district have shifted more towards Democrats' direction in recent weeks, but Republicans are still favored. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report has rated the race "lean Republican."

Gamarra, the politics professor, says the GOP will need to rely on its political infrastructure to pull out a win

"They're not going to win on the issues ... They're going to win on turnout … the enthusiasm is on the Democrat side. But Republicans have a machinery."

entries.title: Major fire breaks out in Alberta after deadly incident at military base
entries.summary: Canada's defense minister said Saturday that people were killed and injured in an incident at a military base in Alberta that caused a major fire.
entries.content:
Major fire breaks out in Alberta after deadly incident at military base

EDMONTON, Alberta — Canada's defense minister said Saturday that people were killed and injured in an incident at a military base in Alberta that caused a major fire, while reports said that large numbers of injured people were being transported to hospitals.

Fire crews scrambled late into the night as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area.

It was not immediately clear how many people were killed or injured, but a doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180 km (120 miles) northwest, told Canada's national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as health-care facilities around the base became "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people needing care.

"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster."

The town of Wainwright, near the base, has about 7,000 residents.

Defense Minister David McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in investigating the incident and described the situation as "very, very active and delicate." He said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information.

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4 p.m. Saturday following reports of a fire in a training area at the base.

Firefighters faced a volatile situation. Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100 kilometres an hour. The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.

By 11 p.m., the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. There was no evacuation order for residents.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.

"Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected," Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier in a social media post.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it was affecting many military personnel.

CFB Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.

Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Carney and the defense minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.

"Pray for Wainwright, everyone," Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.

The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday's referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada. Elections Alberta said two polling locations, in Lloydminster and Vermilion, closed early Saturday and the ballots were transported securely.

entries.title: Oregon governor Tina Kotek reacts to Silver Rail Elementary school shooting
entries.summary: NPR's Joel Rose talks with Oregon Governor Tina Kotek about the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon.
entries.content:
Oregon governor Tina Kotek reacts to Silver Rail Elementary school shooting

NPR's Joel Rose talks with Oregon Governor Tina Kotek about the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon.

JOEL ROSE, HOST:

Just days after the attack on Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend Oregon, new details are emerging about the heroic efforts of bystanders to stop the shooter and about the victims, three children and a teacher who were killed in the attack.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

MIKE KRANTZ: The 5-year-old boy is identified at the request of his family as Rhoam Summer.

ROSE: Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz, speaking at a press conference yesterday.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

KRANTZ: The teacher who was killed and has been identified is 25-year-old Megan Lambert of Bend.

ROSE: A police spokesperson shared a statement from Lambert's family.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

UNIDENTIFIED SPOKESPERSON: Her goal was to be an educator and teach in the school district she loved growing up in. She loved Silver Rail. This was her dream job. Megan was compassionate and had a huge heart. She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs. She was an incredible sister, daughter, niece and granddaughter.

ROSE: And we've learned more about the brave actions of bystanders that day. Again, Police Chief Krantz.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

KRANTZ: A teacher in the classroom threw her cell phone at the suspect and then tackled him and fought to take the firearm from him. She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed.

ROSE: The attacker was followed into the school by a father of two students at Silver Rail.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

KRANTZ: He then went to the classroom where the struggle was underway and fired his weapon, striking the suspect multiple times.

ROSE: Through it all, community members in Bend have been gathering to mourn and to remember the lives of those lost.

UNIDENTIFIED GROUP: (Singing) Now I'm found (ph).

ROSE: Oregon Public Broadcasting reporter Holly Bartholomew was at a vigil last night and talked with Matthew McCarthy, whose mother works at Silver Rail.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)

MATTHEW MCCARTHY: No one really expected it to happen here, but, like, at the same time, it was, like, you know, you always go to it with that thought, like, every morning. Like, my mom works at Silver Rail. She had that thought every day.

ROSE: I want to bring in Oregon governor Tina Kotek now, a Democrat. Welcome to the program, Governor.

TINA KOTEK: Thank you, Joel.

ROSE: First of all, are there any updates you can provide about the investigation into this shooting?

KOTEK: Not at the moment. The press conference yesterday was pretty extensive, and it's an ongoing investigation. And I really appreciate all the outpouring nationally of just well wishes and condolences coming from across the country and people just wanting to know how they can help. And we're still in that, you know, first 48 hours of just trying to understand it. And it's going to be a couple more days before we know all the details.

ROSE: Are there any details you've learned about the other victims which might help us understand, you know, a little bit more about who they were?

KOTEK: Not yet. Everyone is appropriately trying to respect their privacy. There hasn't been the announcements other than the ones you just spoke about. I did have a chance to talk to the mother of Megan Lambert, and obviously, they are heartbroken. Megan was an amazing teacher and volleyball coach loved in the community. And, you know, we have to remember that these events have so much ripple effect across the community, people knowing someone who knows someone or knowing them in all kinds of different contexts. This is such a big shock and pain in the community right now, and people are holding each other up and still just trying to make sense of it, if you even can.

ROSE: Is there any more information you can give us about the shooter's motives? I know that's a question a lot of people are still asking.

KOTEK: I think that's what you see in these situations. People want to know why. We don't have that kind of information. Remember, this was also a child. The shooter was 16 years old. And it's just - you know, we see these patterns, and people want to know what the situation is. It'll be days before we have more information about the background there.

What I'm focused on right now is making sure the school district has what it needs, that the community has what it needs. This is a disaster, I mean, in the most fundamental sense of the word. And so everyone is trying to make sure there are mental health resources, that the immediate needs of some of the people who have been injured are being met.

And this - here's what I know. I hear from other governors, you know, to be a governor, to get this phone call, it's the worst thing you want to have happen. But the outreach from both Republican and Democratic governors alike who have experienced these types of mass shooting incidents in their states, you know, offering advice - this is going to take time, and the thing is we just need to stick with the community who will have a long process of healing from this.

ROSE: Governor Kotek, do you know how the shooter, who was 16 years old, got access to the firearm and ammunition?

KOTEK: I do not have that information. We have - you know, we believe adults should be responsible. We don't know how the gun ended up with the 16-year-old. And - but it's a question everyone is asking.

ROSE: Some outlets are saying that the gun was registered to the mother. Can you confirm that?

KOTEK: I have seen that. I can't confirm that. I am letting law enforcement do their job and getting updates as they have them, but this - you know, it's an ongoing investigation, so I can't speak to that.

ROSE: Oregon gun law does have some exceptions that allow minors to possess long guns if their gun is given to the minor by a parent or a guardian, for example, or with their consent. Do you plan to revisit that in the aftermath of this shooting?

KOTEK: Well, I - you know, as governor, I've been a strong proponent of our gun violence prevention policies, and we've had success here in the state doing evidence-based, reasonable approaches to help people be safe with their firearms. Our law does say that if you are under 18 and have access to that gun, that's because your parent or guardian have given you that permission to have that gun. I think there'll be a lot of questions about that going forward. And I don't - to be honest, it's just too soon to jump into those conversations, but I know that people are going to want to have them.

ROSE: One of the most remarkable things about this tragedy is that a community member with a gun was able to intervene and to kill the shooter. I wonder, has that changed anything about your thinking around gun laws?

KOTEK: Well, I have - you know, you have to do - you have to praise the adults who jumped in. The individual who came into the school after witnessing the 16-year-old coming into the school, the teachers in the classroom fighting to protect the children - it is - and that's - it is both heroic, and you have to say, we shouldn't have to have that. And so, you know, when you have a gun involved, people are going to get hurt. And I know that, you know, the way people have responded in such quick thinking is why there wasn't more death or injury in this situation.

And I want to, you know, praise the Bend-La Pine School District. They have - they've done the things they've needed to do. They had security locks on their doors. They, you know, have been training for these things. You hate to say, we have to train for them, but they were ready in - when it happened to keep as many kids safe as possible. I just want us to get to a place in this country where we don't have to be doing those trainings and those protocols. We just shouldn't have this happening in our schools.

ROSE: You are up for reelection next month, and it is a fairly tight race between you and your Republican counterpart. Should gun control be a key issue, do you think, in this election?

KOTEK: Oh, I don't think any of us should be politicizing this incident. I mean, this is - our job is the stand up for the community right now. And as you have seen across the country, after these events have happened and people have had a chance to think about it, there will be a discussion, probably next year. But right now, I'm focused on the community and making sure they have what they need.

ROSE: You know, Silver Rail Elementary had just done a lockdown drill a few weeks ago. The school's doors were locked. Law enforcement was on the scene quickly.

KOTEK: Yes.

ROSE: You know, the teacher, the other bystanders who intervened - so this is a prepared school, a swift response. And yet, three children and a teacher still lost their lives. Briefly, is there anything else that you plan to do in Oregon to prevent tragedies like this from occurring?

KOTEK: Well, no community should experience this, no parent. And we, as the adults, should continue to think about what we can do differently to keep our young people safe. They should be able to go to school, feel safe, be secure. And like I said, there will be plenty of conversation about the laws we do have on the books, things that we could be doing differently. And we need some space before we can get into that. But what I will say is that I've been proud of Oregon. We approached this in a reasonable, rational way, and that's what we will do going forward when the moments right.

ROSE: Thank you. That is Oregon governor Tina Kotek, a Democrat. Thank you very much for joining me.

KOTEK: Thank you, Joel.

entries.title: Scuffles and fires break out as protesters rally across France, joining students
entries.summary: Demonstrators across France converged with students Saturday to protest rising living costs, as the country's fiscal crisis deepens.
entries.content:
Scuffles and fires break out as protesters rally across France, joining students

PARIS — A car and a newspaper kiosk were set on fire in Paris as police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse violent groups of protesters, while similar tensions erupted Saturday in other big cities on the fringes of nationwide demonstrations against rising living costs and in support of high school students' grievances.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez's office described "a growing number of violent incidents," including assaults on police officers, looting or attempted looting of shops and damage to public buildings. Authorities reported at least 272 arrests across the country, including in Paris.

In the French capital, police used tear gas and water cannons to push back people wearing hoods and masks and throwing fireworks and other objects at officers in the Place de la République, northeast of the Paris city center. Large numbers of riot police were deployed in the square and surrounding streets.

The majority of peaceful protesters joined a march that moved toward northwestern Paris. The crowd chanted France's national anthem as French flags were waved. The chants were accompanied by people playing trumpets and violins.

Meanwhile, police were working to prevent other small groups of protesters from converging on government buildings, Nuñez's office said.

Many metro stations were closed Saturday at police request, including those around the Champs-Elysées and near the presidential palace, parliament and government offices.

Violence hit Lyon, Marseille and other cities

In Lyon, France's third-largest city, where about 20,000 protesters joined the march, fire broke out inside a tourist office. Smoke and flames were seen rising from the building.

In the southern port city of Marseille, some shops and a municipal police station were damaged, while some protesters briefly forced their way into the lobby of City Hall.

"This is unacceptable," Marseille Mayor Benoît Payan told BFM TV, describing the damage in City Hall as "limited."

Nuñez's office also reported violence by masked groups in Rennes, Toulouse, Montpellier and Grenoble, among other cities.

Protesters across France responded to calls on social media to revive the "yellow vest" movement, which emerged in 2018 against social injustice. Demonstrators expressed widespread frustration and anger at the government as gasoline, energy and food prices have spiked in recent months.

Saturday's protests follow weeks of school blockades

Student groups protesting since mid-September through school blockades have urged supporters to join them.

The CGT, one of France's major labor unions, also backed the protests, calling for "higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services that meet people's needs."

In recent weeks, France has seen thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries and schools set on fire as the new school year descended into nationwide student protests that are influencing the country's presidential election campaign and drawing international attention.

Among protesters, particularly gruesome wounds suffered by some teenagers have been blamed on police riot-control weapons. Nuñez suspended the use of a type of police stun grenade against the young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand.

On Tuesday, climate and social justice activist Greta Thunberg joined students at a high school in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis.

entries.title: Pope Leo XIV leaves hospital days after lung cancer surgery
entries.summary: The Pope left Rome's Gemelli Hospital Saturday, days after surgery for lung cancer removed the lower lobe of his right lung. He is currently scheduled to travel to Latin America in November.
entries.content:
Pope Leo XIV leaves hospital days after lung cancer surgery

Pope Leo XIV left Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Saturday afternoon and returned to the Vatican after doctors said he was well enough to be discharged following surgery that removed part of his right lung.

The Vatican press office released a statement outlining details from Dr. Luigi Carbone,the Pope's personal physician, and Professor Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli's chief of thoracic surgery who led the team that operated on Leo. The two doctors said the pope had undergone blood tests and a chest X-ray that morning, with the results confirming his clinical condition meant he could leave hospital.

They said he was expected to lead the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment on Sunday.Video showed Leo waving to well-wishers outside the hospital as he walked out without physical support, flanked by officials and security guards in dark suits.

Before leaving, the pope had celebrated Mass in a room set aside for that purpose on the hospital's 10th floor, according to the press office.

Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni said "the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week." Leo's discharge came on his fifth day in hospital and was sooner than had been expected at the time of the operation's announcement.

A diagnosis made public

Leo, 71, had told crowds in St. Peter's Square last Sunday that doctors had discovered a "localized nodule" in his lung at a "very early stage."

"Following their advice, I have therefore decided to undergo an operation to remove it," he said.

The surgery on Tuesday went further than the nodule, however, with surgeons using a video-assisted technique to remove the lower lobe of the pope's right lung in an operation that lasted about 90 minutes. His doctors said lung tissue examined afterward confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma. With adenocarcinoma making up about 40% of all lung cancers in the U.S., it is the nation's most common form of lung cancer, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America.

That is true among nonsmokers too, according to Dr. Otis Brawley, an oncologist at Johns Hopkins University and former chief medical and scientific officer of the American Cancer Society.

Leo is not known to have smoked, but cancer does run in his family. His mother, Mildred, died of cancer in 1990, and on Tuesday the Vatican announced that his older brother Louis, who lives in Florida, has been hospitalized with a form of cancer.

Encouraging signs

Doctors not involved in the pope's care say the treatment so far points to a cancer that has been caught early.

"The fact that surgery was the first tool that they utilized is a really good sign," Dr. Vin Gupta, a pulmonologist and board member of the American Lung Association, told NPR. "It suggests that they think this is early stage."

Gupta said the fact that doctors removed a larger portion of the lung than first announced is not in itself a bad sign. "People have parts of their lungs removed all the time for all sorts of reasons, and they recover just fine," he said. "And in his case, he's pretty robust at baseline from a health standpoint."

Leo still exercises regularly, playing tennis each week with his personal secretary and riding horses at Castel Gandolfo, the papal retreat to the south of Rome.

The Vatican has not announced any further treatment.

Travels ahead

Leo's office has cleared his public schedule until at least Oct. 20. His next major international trip, set for early November, includes Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where he lived on and off for two decades and holds citizenship.

"He had a minimally invasive surgery," said Dr. Jonathan Villena Vargas, a cardiothoracic surgeon at Weill Cornell Medical Center in New York City. "Because we do this all the time, most patients are allowed to travel about two weeks after the surgery."

Brawley from Johns Hopkins agreed. "I think he can do it," he said, adding that patients in good physical shape who have this type of procedure "very frequently are back to normal in seven to 10 days."

entries.title: Zelenskyy urges support for new US sanctions on Russia after Trump puts them on hold
entries.summary: Zelenskyy described the move as unfortunate, adding it would encourage Russia to continue its assault. Trump told Congress that the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details.
entries.content:
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters Saturday to speak out in defense of new U.S. sanctions against Russia, hours after President Donald Trump signed an executive order pausing a sweeping package of restrictions targeting the Russian economy.

The White House decision has further raised fears that Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow's escalating assaults with winter approaching.

Russian attacks overnight killed at least four people, including an ambulance driver, and wounded dozens, officials said. Ukrainian drones killed a woman in a Russian border region and disrupted flights at Moscow's airports, according to Russian authorities.

In a statement on social media, Zelenskyy described Trump's move to put sanctions on hold as unfortunate, but did not directly criticize the U.S. leader despite deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington in recent days.

"A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote.

Later, in audio clips answering journalists' questions, Zelenskyy thanked Democrats and Republicans who backed the legislation and praised its bipartisan support. He said blocking it would encourage Russia to continue killing and do nothing to bring the war to an end.

He also added that limiting Ukraine's ability to retaliate against Russian attacks would not bring peace.

"Nevertheless, we very much hope — and I personally hope — that the president of the United States of America will do everything possible to make Putin stop the killing, stop the attacks on our energy infrastructure, and end this war," he said.

Critics say Trump's decision helps Putin

Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling Russia's 4 1/2-year-old war against Ukraine. The bill had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.

Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation.

The president told Congress that the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who co-drafted the bill, said in a statement that Trump was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies."

"These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Blumenthal said.

Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.

Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."

The decision has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine — without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump's war on Iran.

Kyiv says Moscow carried out a 'massive' energy strike

Zelenskyy also said Saturday that Moscow had carried out a massive strike on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 sites across the country.

"The sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia's strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences," he said.

Ukraine's air force said that Russian forces launched four cruise missiles and 332 attack drones overnight. All of the missiles and 289 of the drones had been suppressed or destroyed, it said.

Russia's heavy bombardment of the power grid ahead of winter has been an annual feature of the war, aimed at wearing down Ukraine's appetite for the fight by denying civilians heat and running water. Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in the coming months.

Russian attacks killed three people in the Ukrainian city of Sloviansk, Vadym Liakh, head of the city military administration, said Saturday. Writing on social media, Liakh said that two apartment blocks were partially destroyed and other homes damaged.

A Russian strike also killed an ambulance driver in Ukraine's Kherson region, head of the local military administration Yaroslav Shanko said. The strike, which used guided bombs, wounded at least 33 others, he said.

Ukrainian drones kill 1, ground hundreds of flights at Moscow airports

Elsewhere, a Russian woman was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in the Russian border region of Belgorod, local officials said.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday that its forces had shot down 610 Ukrainian drones overnight over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that more than 100 drones were shot down en route to the Russian capital. More than 350 flights were canceled or delayed at Moscow's airports, local media reported, as planes were grounded in response to incoming drones.

The Kremlin announced Saturday that Russian President Vladimir Putin had approved a government program to help restore trade and logistics facilities damaged in drone attacks.

entries.title: Perspective: Midterm money madness
entries.summary: Campaign ad spending has topped $10 billion this election cycle, as voters struggle to afford groceries and gas.
entries.content:
Perspective: Midterm money madness

Campaign spending for these midterm elections passed 10 billion dollars this week, according to the tracking group AdImpact.

Maybe we should repeat that number: $10 billion dollars.

The senate race in Ohio, for example, has already cost more than $460 million in combined ad spending. The Texas Senate race has surpassed half a billion. Then there's $260 million more in the Maine Senate race.

The most expensive House race in the country isn't in California or New York, but Michigan's 7th congressional district with nearly $60 million in ads. Contests in Iowa and Florida are just under $50 million apiece.

There are limits on personal campaign contributions in the United States--but, since the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision in 2010, no limits on donations to "super PACs," which can publicly support or oppose candidates but can't directly coordinate with campaigns. Rich donors have used that ruling to steer hundreds of millions of dollars to support both parties, up and down the ballot. Elon Musk alone has given $276 million to Republican groups, just since July. George Soros has given more than $100 million dollars to Democrats this election cycle.

Meanwhile, voters, whom politicians are trying to win over with all these ads, tell pollsters and reporters that their top issues this fall are the economy and the cost of living. Inflation is up; gas prices have spiked since the start of the Iran war; groceries cost a third more than they did in 2019.

It is hard not to wonder: what could those hundreds of millions of ad dollars accomplish if they went toward food, gas, or shelter for those in need, or to help people with health care costs? Could some of it pay for school nurses, music teachers, and librarians? Subsidize addiction care? Clean up public parks?

Maybe a candidate could win support these days by declaring, "And I vow to spend less money on my campaign than my opponent!" After all, as the Los Angeles Dodgers might remind us this week, spending the most money doesn't always deliver victory.

entries.title: Fraud, affordability and Trump policies drive friction in Minnesota Senate debate
entries.summary: The major party candidates for Minnesota's U.S. Senate seat faced off in an hourlong debate Friday on MPR News with fraud, affordability and fallout from the Trump administration's policies as key points of friction.
entries.content:
Fraud, affordability and Trump policies drive friction in Minnesota Senate debate

The major party candidates for Minnesota's U.S. Senate seat faced off in an hourlong debate Friday on MPR News with fraud, affordability and fallout from the Trump administration's policies as key points of friction.

SCOTT SIMON, HOST:

Tight Senate races in Texas, Iowa and Kansas are getting a lot of attention during this year's midterm elections. But Minnesota also has a close race, and Peter Cox from Minnesota Public Radio joins us now. Thanks so much for being with us.

PETER COX, BYLINE: Good morning, Scott.

SIMON: Please tell us who's running and why this race has maybe been a little overlooked nationally.

COX: So Peggy Flanagan, a progressive Democrat who's been lieutenant governor in Minnesota for the last eight years, is up against Republican Michele Tafoya, who spent years as a sideline reporter for Monday Night Football and Sunday Night Football. And they're battling for a seat that's been held by Democrats since 2009. Recent polls have shown the two neck and neck, though Flanagan had a 4% edge in the most recent one.

But normally, such a tight margin would mean political parties would be pouring money into this race. But that's not what's happening here. This election, Republicans are facing challenges in what would be reliably red states, so they've been putting their money into shoring up those races instead. And that seems to be a big reason why Minnesota's race has been much quieter, even though it's one of several that could determine which party controls the U.S. Senate.

SIMON: President Trump indicated this week he might make a trip to Minnesota. How big a factor has President Trump been in this race?

COX: Yeah. Like many of these midterm races we're seeing nationwide, President Trump is a major factor. Tafoya, who has never held public office before, said when she announced her candidacy she'd be honored to have his endorsement. But in recent months, she's tried to distance herself from Trump. And that became tougher this week when Trump was speaking at a campaign rally in Ohio, and he railed against members of Minnesota's Somali community who he said were looting Minnesota welfare programs. He then implored people to get out and vote for Tafoya.

During a debate yesterday, Tafoya was asked whether she'd campaign with Trump if he comes to Minnesota, and she didn't answer the question. Peggy Flanagan has consistently said Tafoya would be a lapdog for Trump and was quick to point out how Tafoya only recently has tried to distance herself from the president in this campaign.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

PEGGY FLANAGAN: Minnesotans are smarter than this new version of Michele Tafoya who has shown up in the final weeks of this campaign. Give me a break.

SIMON: Governor Tim Walz's administration has gotten a lot of heat over the fraud that you mentioned. Has this extended to Lieutenant Governor Flanagan, who, after all, is his second in command?

COX: Yes. About 70 people have been convicted of bilking millions of dollars from state programs in the last few years, and questions have been raised about why the Walz administration didn't respond more quickly. During the debate, Tafoya was quick to point the finger at Flanagan.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

MICHELE TAFOYA: This historic fraud happened under her watch, and suddenly, she's looking out for Medicaid and SNAP? Sell it to someone else, Peggy.

COX: Now, Flanagan says the issue was not under her purview as lieutenant governor.

SIMON: The Trump administration cited this fraud as one reason for the increased immigration crackdowns in Minnesota last winter. Is that enforcement surge playing a role in this race?

COX: Well, the monthlong surge has been eclipsed recently by other issues like the economy and cost of living, but it's definitely still resonating. And Flanagan has commended the large-scale protests against ICE in Minnesota and has called for the agency to be dismantled. Now, Tafoya has criticized the rollout of the enforcement surge and called the fatal shootings of Americans Renee Good and Alex Pretti by immigration agents devastating. But she also criticized the protests and said local leaders encouraged them.

SIMON: Peter, any signs this race might get a last-minute influx of outside spending, as we've seen elsewhere?

COX: Well, the president talking about this race this week, saying he might visit, could put it more front and center for some. But we haven't seen any big changes in political spending here in the last few days. About two weeks ago, U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune came to stump for Tafoya at a farm in Southern Minnesota. And when he was asked whether the political action committee he helps run - the Senate Leadership Fund - would give Tafoya a funding boost, he was noncommittal. And we still haven't seen much national money flowing in to support either candidate. We're a little more than two weeks out from the election, so the runway for that kind of investment in this race is getting pretty short.

SIMON: Peter Cox of Minnesota Public Radio. Thanks so much for being with us.

COX: You're welcome.

(SOUNDBITE OF CHROMEO SONG, "CABIN FEVER")

entries.title: Dozens of critically endangered orangutans rescued from Indonesian wildfires
entries.summary: Rescuers in Indonesia have saved dozens of orangutans from wildfires. The critically endangered species is fighting for their lives and habitats during this deadly wildfire season.
entries.content:
Dozens of critically endangered orangutans rescued from Indonesian wildfires

Rescuers in Indonesia have saved dozens of orangutans from wildfires. The critically endangered species is fighting for their lives and habitats during this deadly wildfire season.

SCOTT SIMON, HOST:

The endangered orangutans of Borneo are holding on, but just barely. This year's super El Nino has made Indonesia extra hot and dry, and wildfires have burned 2.2 million acres of land this season.

JAMARTIN SIHITE: And it's destroyed the orangutan habitat, orangutan home.

SIMON: That's Jamartin Sihite, chairman of the Borneo Orangutan Survival Foundation, trying to pull orangutans to safety away from the fires and smoke. Huge swaths of orangutan habitats are burning.

SIHITE: If I look at the maps from the fire and the map from the population of orangutan in the forest, I thought more than 50 to 60% of the habitat of orangutan now getting burned or at least got impact from the smoke.

SIMON: The humans who are breathing the smoke will be vulnerable to asthma, heart attacks and even a shortened life expectancy, and orangutans, who share so much of our DNA, face the same health crises.

SIHITE: Like a human, acute respiratory infection. This is the biggest problems now for human and for the orangutan.

SIMON: He says that at least humans can wear masks on our own. Orangutans cannot. Sihite's organization is one of several in the area working to rescue and rehabilitate orangutans who are being affected by wildfires. They ran a similar rescue operation in 2015 when massive forest and peatland fires burned inside Indonesia.

Wendy Erb is a biological anthropologist who specializes in primate behavior. She's watching these fires from Ithaca, New York, but in 2015, she was in a field station in Borneo studying orangutan behavior.

WENDY ERB: My very favorite orangutan showed up in front of camp, and I couldn't resist just spending one more day with him. So I extended my stay by a day, and then that day turned into an extension of a month as the fires decided to pop up in our study area that very day that I was supposed to leave.

SIMON: Like many who are fighting today's fires, Erb and her team dug small wells into the ground that could be used with a generator to pump water up from several meters below the peatland, till finally, a month in, they got enough rain to put out the fires and to flee. But even when the fires are gone, Sihite says the survival struggle is not over.

SIHITE: After the fire, we still face the problems in the forest. We will face, like, scarcity of food because there is no pollination. There is no fruit.

SIMON: Sihite's team rescued a 5-year-old female orangutan called Novita last month. Novita was found in the forest canopy surrounded by smoke and flame. Twenty percent of her body was burned, including her hands and feet. She was treated with a nebulizer to help her breathe and is now recovering at a rehabilitation center.

How many like Novita still need help? Rescue agencies have pulled dozens of orangutans out of danger, including multiple mothers with infants and young males who had been stranded. They are still trying to figure out how to help the 104,000 Borneo orangutans that are left in Indonesia. There is no doubt that the fires are destructive, but Erb believes the orangutans will find a way to survive.

ERB: Because orangutans are quite resilient and pretty flexible, as well as incredibly intelligent and ecologically resourceful, they really can sort of make a go at even a pretty degraded habitat.

SIMON: That's biological anthropologist Wendy Erb, who studies orangutan behavior at Cornell University. We also heard from Jamartin Sihite, chairman of the Borneo Orangutan Survival Foundation.

(SOUNDBITE OF TOWER OF POWER'S "SQUIB CAKES")

entries.title: Decades after apartheid, South Africans seek justice for crimes of the past
entries.summary: More than three decades after the end of apartheid, families of victims of some of the worst crimes of South Africa's pastare still fighting for justice. As survivors and perpetrators grow older, a new wave of legal efforts is seeking truth, accountability and reparations before it's too late.
entries.content:
Decades after apartheid, South Africans seek justice for crimes of the past

SHARPEVILLE, South Africa – Paulina Mathinye gestures with anguish at the rows of garbage-strewn graves, overrun with weeds, in the cemetery where her father is buried.

"Look at that, where they sleep," she says of the dozens of Black protesters buried here, all of whom were killed when police opened fire on March 21, 1960 in what became one of the bloodiest days in apartheid history.

"Why are they dirty? It's a disgrace," says the 71-year-old grandmother, who wears a floral dress and a smart sunhat.

The cemetery, like much else in this visibly poor township about an hour's drive from Johannesburg, has been left to decay. But Mathinye notes that for one day a year at least, when South Africa's political elite descend to commemorate the massacre, the graveyard is spotless. The anniversary is a public holiday known as Human Rights Day.

"I'm still angry. My anger comes out because that's the day my father was shot," says Mathinye, who was just five years old at the time.

She says her father's part in what became a turning point in the struggle against apartheid has not been sufficiently recognized by the current democratic government.

And she says she wants justice – however delayed.

That's why she's signed up to take part in a potential class action lawsuit 66 years later, along with Sharpeville survivors and the families of Sharpeville victims.

At least 69 people were shot by police that day. They had been demonstrating against the country's pass laws – which restricted black people's movements and where they could live and work.

While it's unclear if any perpetrators are still alive, those taking part in the case hope it could lead to reparations.

But first, the group's lawyers must challenge an apartheid-era law that continues to block their efforts to seek legal redress. The law remains in force decades after apartheid ended and a Black-majority government took power.

In September they filed an application in the Gauteng High Court challenging the continued existence of the Indemnity Act 61 of 1961. If the court finds the law unconstitutional, and also certifies a class action for survivors and dependants of those killed, then claims for individual damages could follow.

Mathinye says the repercussions of that day in 1960 have affected her whole life.

Without her father, the main breadwinner, she couldn't finish school. That, in turn, affected the lives of her children and grandchildren.

"So we struggled a lot. And we are still struggling now, because nothing has been happening," she told NPR.

If the case goes ahead and succeeds, Mathinye says she'll use any money from reparations to fix up her modest home and pay for her four grandkids' educations.

Part of a wider trend

The Sharpeville case is just one in a new wave of legal efforts that are seeking truth, accountability and reparations for apartheid-era crimes before it's too late.

"It's crucial that these issues of deep injustice are properly dealt with and that South Africa confronts them and does not sweep them under the carpet," says Daniel Leader, an international human rights lawyer advising the South African legal team representing the Sharpeville survivors and families.

Other cases include a court ruling last year that found South Africa's first Nobel Peace Prize laureate, Chief Albert Luthuli, was beaten to death by apartheid police in 1967.

Luthuli, the former leader of the African National Congress — Nelson Mandela's party — had previously been ruled to have died after being struck by a train. The new ruling overturned the finding of an earlier inquest.

The inquest into the 1985 killings of four anti-apartheid activists known as the "Cradock Four" has also been reopened. The activists were abducted and killed by apartheid security forces near the Eastern Cape town of Cradock. Although the officers involved are all dead, the victims' families hope the inquest will establish who ordered the killings.

And the inquest into the torture and death of Steve Biko, the iconic Black Consciousness leader who died in police detention in 1977, has also returned to court.

"It's very clear that the murder of Steve Biko was exactly that, murder," Biko's son Nkosinathi told media in September at the reopened inquest. "We hope that this inquest will eventually get to this very certain, unambiguous finding."

The original inquest in 1977 heard from members of the security branch who said Biko had fallen and hit his head in a "scuffle with security police."

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), a court-like restorative justice body set up in the 1990s to uncover the truth about human rights violations during apartheid, re-examined the Biko case.

It denied amnesty to security officers who testified, saying they hadn't been truthful. That essentially cleared the way for possible prosecutions, but they never happened.

In fact, hundreds of the TRC's recommendations for prosecutions were delayed or never pursued. Last year, President Cyril Ramaphosa established a formal inquiry to investigate whether the recommendations were deliberately shelved.

The inquiry is looking into whether there was a secret deal between the old leaders of the apartheid regime and the country's new Black leaders not to prosecute cases in the interests of reconciliation. Its findings are due in December.

Back at the Sharpeville cemetery, Paulina Mathinye and three other descendants of those killed in the massacre, pause in front of a memorial plaque before exiting the graveyard.

Vincent Thamae, from the NGO, Voices of Sharpeville which works with survivors and descendants asks that they take leave of the dead.

"We ask of those who are sleeping here to be with us as we pursue justice for them," he says.
